Neonatal Indian peafowl chicks emerge from eggs incubated at 37 °C [T = 37 °C] after a developmental period of 29 days [ab = 29 days], a duration typical of large galliform birds. At hatching, these precocial chicks display a wet weight at birth of 120 grams [Wwb = 120 grams], representing a modest initial investment relative to the substantial adult dimensions the species ultimately achieves. Field studies indicate that females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 3.1 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 3.1 kilograms], though individuals at the upper end of the distribution can approach 4 kilograms, while males, which are markedly larger and characterized by elongated train feathers, reach an ultimate wet weight of 4 kilograms [Wwi = 4 kilograms]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is among the most extreme observed in the Phasianidae and is tightly linked to the species' lek-based mating system, where larger males with more elaborate plumage enjoy higher reproductive success. The energetic demands of supporting such dimorphism are reflected in both the protracted growth period and the differential timing of developmental milestones between the sexes, a pattern that underscores the evolutionary trade-offs inherent in this species' life-history strategy.

Under the warm thermal conditions typical of the active foraging and display periods for this species, approximately 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the development of young peafowl proceeds along a well-defined trajectory. The chicks, following their emergence from the shell, undergo a remarkably rapid exotrophic transition and are capable of leaving the nest site and following their mother within just 3 days after hatching [tx = 3 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This early nest departure, a form of precocial development, allows the brood to exploit dispersed food resources and reduces vulnerability to nest predators that rely on olfactory or auditory cues. The pace of somatic growth in the months following hatching is considerable, with males in particular investing heavily in skeletal and muscular development to support their eventual large body size. During this period, at the ambient temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C] that characterizes their active season, young peafowl reach sexual maturity at approximately 200 days after hatching [tp = approximately 200 days after hatching]. This timing is notably close to the point at which individuals have achieved near-adult skeletal dimensions, though the full elaboration of the male's ornamental train requires additional months of feather growth and molting cycles. This delay between physiological and functional reproductive maturity reflects a strategy in which somatic investment precedes full reproductive engagement.

Reproductive activity in free-ranging populations of Pavo cristatus, measured under field conditions at a mean ambient temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], is characterized by a modest fecundity relative to many other galliforms. This deferred reproduction until two years of age is common among long-lived bird species that employ a polygynous mating system, as it allows individuals to accumulate the resources and social capital necessary to successfully rear or sire offspring.

The lifespan of the Indian peafowl is considerable for a bird of its body mass, particularly when individuals are protected from predation and provided with consistent food resources. Captive records and long-term field studies indicate that the maximum documented longevity reaches approximately 23.2 years [am = approximately 23.2 years] at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], a figure that places this species among the longer-lived members of the Phasianidae and confirms an approximate longevity of 23.2 years [am = 23.2 years] under protected conditions. Such life-history characteristics are consistent with what we might expect for a species occupying a relatively stable, resource-predictable environment where adult survival is high and competition for nesting sites and display territories is intense.
